disease_label_per_paper: Occupational sodium cyanide poisoning during nickel and chrome plating tank cleaning

history: two prior attacks of nephritic colic
no known cardiovascular history or hypertension

presentation_summary: A 41-year-old man working in nickel and chrome plating entered a factory tank to clean it with sodium cyanide powder dissolved for metal degreasing.
He was exposed for about 15 minutes before colleagues found him unconscious in the tank; firefighters detected cyanide above 20 ppm, the maximum displayed by their apparatus.

On firefighter arrival he could not speak or follow simple commands but breathed spontaneously; four minutes later he had a generalized seizure followed by cardiac arrest, reversed after 2 minutes of CPR.
Twenty minutes after discovery the SMUR team recorded GCS 6, sinus rhythm 100/min, blood pressure 80/60 mmHg, pink skin, and a second generalized seizure responsive to 1 mg IV clonazepam.
He was intubated and ventilated with 100% oxygen; 35 minutes after discovery he received 5 g hydroxocobalamin before transfer.
At hospital admission 120 minutes after collapse, while post-antidote and ventilated, ABG showed pH 7.18, lactate 7.6 mEq/L, PaCO2 45 mmHg, PaO2 380 mmHg, bicarbonate 15 mmol/L, and HbCO 1.1%.
He ultimately received 10 g total hydroxocobalamin and hyperbaric oxygen, was extubated 30 hours after collapse, discharged home after one week, and returned to work two weeks after the accident.

quality_warnings: Only this case JSON was added; no disease distillation or axis registry file was modified.
Ranking evidence uses occupational sodium cyanide exposure, environmental cyanide detection, acute coma/GCS, seizures, cardiac arrest, hypotension, intubation, and acute acidosis/lactate.
Hydroxocobalamin response, thiocyanate after treatment, red urine, hyperbaric oxygen, extubation, discharge, return to work, and rhabdomyolysis course are non-ranking.
ABG and lactate values were measured after prehospital hydroxocobalamin and may underestimate peak cyanide physiology.
